edges.effect_quant: The best catch-up data still point to meaningful precancer protection when vaccination starts in the mid-teen years or early adulthood. In Australia's national cohort, one dose was associated with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.65 for CIN2, CIN3, AIS, or cancer versus no vaccination, and a large US case-control study found a rate ratio of 0.52 for CIN2+ when at least three doses began at ages 14 to 17.
edges.population: adolescent girls and young women receiving catch-up HPV vaccination after the earliest routine vaccination window
edges.mechanism: Catch-up HPV vaccination reduces acquisition and persistence of oncogenic HPV types, lowering the chance that cervical infection progresses to CIN2, CIN3, adenocarcinoma in situ, or related high-grade lesions before cancer develops.
edges.summary: The evidence supports a real protective effect for catch-up HPV vaccination against high-grade cervical lesions, especially when vaccination starts before the early 20s. Australian and US population studies both show lower CIN2+ and CIN3+ rates among vaccinated young women, although the benefit weakens when first-dose timing is later.
edges.caveats: This is mostly observational evidence, so screening behavior, sexual-health differences, and age at first dose still matter. The strongest protection appears in women vaccinated in adolescence or by around age 20, with less convincing benefit when catch-up begins at age 21 or older.

evidence.citation: Brotherton JML et al 2019 Papillomavirus Res
evidence.notes: Is one dose of human papillomavirus vaccine as effective as three?: A national cohort analysis.

effect_quant.comparator: one vaccine dose versus no vaccination for CIN2, CIN3, adenocarcinoma in situ, or cervical cancer in the Australian national cohort
